analytic.title: Schedulability Analysis of Multi-Frame Messages over Controller Area Networks with Mixed-queues

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The Controller Area Network (CAN) is one of the most widely utilized real-time communication networks, which has plenty of applications especially in automotive industry. Many works have been proposed regarding the CAN schedulability analysis which is very important for guaranteeing the safety and reliability of hard real-time systems. Most of the existing analysis methods assume a periodic message model, and some of them take sporadic messages into account. However, for some applications, message transmissions may follow a specific pattern instead of repeating the same transmission period by period, where applying the existing methods may include much pessimism. In this paper, we apply the Multi-Frame task model, which is first proposed by Mok and Chen in [1], on messages over a CAN-based system with mixed message queues. In this preliminary work, the analysis is based on some specific assumptions. A more general analysis will be investigated in our later works.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The Controller Area Network (CAN) has been widely utilized in many industrial areas, such as the automotive industry, aerospace, industrial automation and so on. In a CAN based real-time system, different nodes, which are denoted Electronic Control Units (ECU) in an automotive system, use the CAN bus to transmit messages. Each message is usually associated with a unique identifier, which is commonly considered as the fixed priority of this message. A message with a higher priority is usually delivered ahead of a lower priority message. More information can be found in the standard ISO 11898 [2].

In a hard real-time system, the timing constraints are supposed to be strictly satisfied. Otherwise, the performance of the system may be dramatically decreased, furthermore, a constraint violation may even incur a catastrophic problem in some unfortunate cases. Therefore, a schedulability analysis, which focuses on the issue of deadline missing, is very important for system designers. Generally, a system is considered to be schedulable when all tasks can always be finished within their respective deadlines. In the real-time network scheduling, the transmission of a message can be considered as a task in the above systems.

A number of works have been proposed regarding the schedulability analysis of CAN messages. In [3], Tindell et al. first introduced a worst-case response time analysis of CAN messages, which is based on the traditional response time analysis of fixed priority tasks developed by Joseph et al. in [4]. However, the analysis in [3] may produce optimistic results due to the internal influences of successive instances of an analyzed message [5]. Therefore, in [6], Davis et al. proposed a revised response time analysis method for CAN messages. Some other CAN analysis methods have also been published with respect to different system factors. In [7], the authors provided a response time analysis for CAN messages with offsets. Davis et al. [8] presented another analysis method, where some ECUs can employ First-In-First-Out (FIFO) message queues while the others employ priority-based queues. Later on, Mubeen et al. [9] extended the work in [7] and [8] to support mixed CAN messages, where the messages can be periodic (time triggered) and sporadic (event triggered) at the same time. Moreover, some stochastic methods (e.g. [10] [11]) and statistical approaches (e.g. [12] [13]) have also been proposed. In most of the above methods, the maximum transmission time of a message is usually assumed to be constant for each period (i.e. the traditional periodic message model).

However, for some applications, the maximum transmission time of a message may vary within different periods but still follow a certain pattern from a general point of view. For example, an ECU cyclically reads data from three sensors, and sends the collected data to another ECU through the same message flow. In other words, the ECU respectively reads the first sensor at time t (t > 0), the second sensor at time t + T (T > 0), and the third sensor at time t + 2T . For each period (T ), the ECU only reads one sensor, and it repeats this cyclic ordered pattern. The classical periodic message model performs well, when the data from the three sensors have identical sizes. However, sometimes the data from different sensors may have varied sizes. In this case, using identicalsized frames may obviously cause a waste of bandwidth, because the payload of a frame must be able to contain the largest data from the sensors, which means that a frame carrying a smaller data needs to be filled with unused bits. On another hand, if the size of a frame can vary according to different collected data, to apply the above analysis methods, we need to use the maximum transmission time of the largest frame to bound all the frames in the same message flow. As a result, using those methods may result in much pessimism. Therefore, we need to use a more adaptive model to capture the features of this type of messages, and provide an acceptable schedulability analysis.

In [1], Mok and Chen first introduced the Multi-Frame (MF) model, which generalized the well-known periodic task model presented in [14]. In this model, each task executes periodically following a specific pattern, where each pattern is formed by a number of successive instances with identical inter-arrival times. A utilization based schedulability analysis has also been presented in [1] assuming a preemptive fixed priority scheduling policy. Some other analysis methods have also been proposed with respect of the MF task scheduling, including both utilization based (e.g. [15]) and response time based (e.g. [16]) analysis.

To the best of our knowledge, no work has been done regarding applying the MF model on CAN messages. Therefore, in this paper, we use the MF model to characterize messages transmitted in a CAN-based system with mixed message queues, and a sufficient response time based schedulability analysis is presented.

The rest of this paper is structured as follows. Section II introduces the system model and the assumptions used in this paper. In Section III, we illustrate our preliminary response time based schedulability analysis along with the corresponding proofs. Finally, in Section IV, we conclude the paper and discuss some thoughts about future works.
Due to page limitation, some proofs and examples are omitted in this paper. The corresponding details can be found in our technical report [17].

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL AND ASSUMPTIONS A. System model
div.p: In this paper, the system under analysis consists of a number of ECUs and a shared CAN bus. As presented in [8], an ECU can employ a Priority based message Queue (PQ) or a FIFO message Queue (FQ). The network may include several ECUs with different message queues. Once a task generates a message frame, this frame will be sent to the message queue within its located ECU. When a frame becomes the head of the corresponding message queue, it will be able to compete in the bus arbitration with the head frames from other ECUs. A frame will be delivered if it succeeds in the bus arbitration (i.e. it has the highest priority among all the competitors within this arbitration round).

div.head: B. Multi-frame model
div.p: In [1], the authors proposed a multi-frame model for task scheduling, where the execution times of a task change periodically based on a specific pattern. In other words, each task has a large cycle (i.e. a larger period), and the task executions repeat periodically for different cycles. Each cycle can be divided into several smaller equal periods, and the execution times within different periods may differ from each other. In this paper, we apply this model on messages transmitted over a CAN bus. Note that, in this paper, a message denotes a message flow (i.e. similar concept of a task in [1]), and each instance of the message is called a frame (i.e. similar concept of a job in [1]).
A multi-frame message M i can be characterized as
div.formula: M i = ( - → C i , T i , J i , D i , P i ). The array - → C i = {C i,1 ,C i,2 ,...C i,N i } contains the
div.p: transmission times of all N i consecutive frames of message M i within one large cycle. The period T i is the inter-arrival time between each two successive frames, therefore, the length of a large cycle is N i • T i . The release jitter J i denotes the maximum time duration between the arrival and the release of a frame. Each message has an identical relative deadline D i for all of its frames. Under the regular hard real-time constraints, a message set is defined as schedulable only when the worstcase transmission delays of all the messages never exceed their deadlines. In this paper, we only consider the scenarios with constrained deadlines (i.e. D i ≤ T i ). The arbitration of a CAN bus transmission depends on the priorities of different messages. The priority P i of a message is associated with its fixed IDentifier (ID), which means that each message has a unique priority. The lower an ID is, the higher the priority is. All the above message parameters have been illustrated in an example shown in Figure 1.

In [1], the multi-frame model is assumed to satisfy the Accumulative Monotonic (AM) property. A multi-frame message M i is considered as satisfying the AM property, when an integer k (k = 1, ..., N i ) exists such that the cumulative transmission time requested by m successive frames, which start with the k th frame, is always equal to or greater than that after the arrival of any other frame of M i . div.head: C. Assumptions
div.p: The analysis presented in this paper is based on the following assumptions:

1) All the multi-frame messages in the analyzed system are assumed to satisfy the AM property. 2) Each message has a fixed unique priority which is shared by all its frames. 3) The deadline of a message is assumed to be less than or equal to its period (i.e. D i ≤ T i ).

div.head: A. Analysis for messages with constrained deadlines
div.p: In this section, we present the worst-case transmission delay analysis of messages with limited deadlines. In other words, we assume that the deadlines of all the messages in the network do not exceed their periods (i.e. D i ≤ T i ). The analysis is divided into two parts according to different message queues.

1) Priority-queued messages: Before a frame in an ECU equiped with a priority based message queue starts its transmission, it may need to wait for the transmission of at most one frame from a message with lower priority and the transmission of messages with higher priorities. Therefore, the transmission delay of the k th frame F i,k of message M i is composed of three parts: the transmission time of the frame itself C i,k ; the blocking delay B i,k caused by the frames with lower priorities due to the non-preemptive transmission mechanism; and the interference delay I i,k incurred by the messages with higher priorities.

The transmission time of a frame may vary due to different payload sizes and varied stuffing-bits (more detailed information of an analysis regarding bit-stuffing can be found in [10]). Unlike the Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) of a task, the maximum transmission time of a frame is much more predictable due to less variance. Here we assume that C i,k is the worst-case transmission time of frame F i,k with the maximum number of stuffing-bits.

As presented in [6] and [8], a frame may experience the maximum blocking delay, when it is released at the beginning of a busy period which starts immediately after the largest lower priority frame begins its transmission. In this case, the maximum blocking delay will be equal to the transmission time of this lower priority frame, that is called direct blocking in [8]. However, sometimes the previous frame of message M i may cause a similar delay by postponing a higher priority message, which is defined as push-through blocking (see more details in [6]). In this case, the blocking delay can be bounded by the maximum transmission time of the previous frame (denoted by preC(F i,k )). As discussed in [6], a message can only experience either a direct blocking or a push-through blocking. Therefore, the maximum blocking delay of frame F i,k can be computed as

3) Schedulability test: The procedure of the schedulability test has been presented in Algorithm 1, where the basic idea is the same as the analysis presented in [8].

As presented above, in this paper, we use the same idea proposed in [8] that the buffering time of a FIFO-queued message M j (i.e. the queueing time from entering the message queue until it starts to compete in the bus arbitration) is considered as an additional jitter f j . Due to this abstraction, the consideration of the potentially complex interactions between FIFO queues of different ECUs can be avoided. Moreover, this additional jitter f j can be bounded by
div.formula: f j = ŵ j -C MIN j -J j (28)
div.p: where C MIN j is the minimum transmission time of frames in message M j .

A circular dependency problem may occur, if messages in different FIFO queues have interleaved priorities (see the example in [8]). Fortunately, we notice that Eq. 14 and Eq. 27 are monotonically non-decreasing regarding the buffering times (i.e. f j ), and Eq. 28 is monotonically non-decreasing regarding the response time ŵ j which is computed by Eq. 27. Therefore, we can similarly utilize the solution presented in [8], that is to iteratively calculate the response time ŵ j for each message M j until the buffering time f j reaches a convergence (i.e. the boolean condition repeat in Algorithm 1 stays as f alse). Based on this outer loop iteration approach (Algorithm 1 line 3-22), we can compute upper bounds for the worstcase transmission delays of all messages in the analyzed network. Once the result of a message exceeds its deadline, the algorithm can be aborted (Algorithm 1 line 8-10 or line [17][18][19].

This schedulability analysis is a sufficient but not necessary test due to some pessimism involved in the calculation. One type of pessimism is caused by the selected bound of the pushthrough blocking delay (Eq. 5 and Eq. 18), because this bound for an analyzed frame F i,k only occurs when the response time of the previous frame equates to the period. ŵi ← Eq. 27 (M i ) In this paper, we present a sufficient schedulability analysis for Multi-Frame messages over Controller Area Networks (CAN) with mixed message queues. In this analysis, a message is characterized by the MF model which is a generalization of the traditional periodic task model, and it can be queued in either a FIFO-based or a priority-based queue.

This preliminary work is based on some specific assumptions such as constrained deadlines and the AM property, which may really limit the applicability of the analysis. Therefore, in our following work, we will relax those unrealistic assumptions. On another hand, we also plan to apply the Generalized Multi-Frame (GMF) model [18], which is a generalization of the MF model, on CAN messages.

Another potential continuous work is to extend the endto-end delay analysis of multi-frame messages from CAN to CAN-Ethernet integrated networks. As far as we know, these 1 While computing ŵi , the computed queueing delay QD i (Eq. 20, Eq. 21 or Eq. 22) is assigned to QD MAX i integrated networks are gaining more and more attention in industry due to the larger capability and higher flexibility.

Moreover, many applications are soft timing-constrained, which means that the system can afford some deadline missing within a certain range. As a result, deterministic analysis may result in overly unnecessary pessimism for some cases. Therefore, to develop a corresponding probabilistic analysis may be more interesting for this type of applications.
